sessions.wtr_new_notes:
READ each word as it appears. -ACY means quality, state.
accuracy - accurate means correct and exact + -ACY means quality or state: the quality of being correct and exact.
adequacy - adequate means enough for a need + -ACY means quality or state: the state of being enough for the need.
candidacy - candidate means a person seeking selection + -ACY means state: the state of being a candidate.
delicacy - delicate means fine or fragile + -ACY means quality: the quality of being delicate.
literacy - literate means able to read and write + -ACY means state: the state of being literate.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Extend last week's adverbial work by adding a given adverbial to a plain sentence.
PREP: Have whiteboards ready before the I do.

i_do.title: Add useful detail
i_do.rule: An adverbial adds when, where, how or why. Put it at the front or end; use a comma after a fronted adverbial.
i_do.example: The circuit worked. + during the test -> During the test, the circuit worked.
items: During the test tells WHEN.
It moved to the front, so it takes a comma.
i_do.routine: Eyes on me - watch the addition
i_do.footer: Add the detail, then check the comma
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: During the test, the circuit worked.
1. SAY: "An adverbial tells when, where, how or why. I can add it to make a plain sentence more precise."
2. MODEL: Move during the test to the front. SAY: "It tells when, so I add a comma behind it."
3. ASK: "What does during the test tell us?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: when.
4. ASK: "Why is there a comma?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: the adverbial is at the front.
TRAP: adding the words but missing the comma. Fix: reread the opening detail, hear the pause, then add the comma.
---
Purpose: restate the rule and model adding a given adverbial. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar]

we_do.title: Add it at the end
we_do.rule: Add the given adverbial where it makes sense. An adverbial at the end usually needs no comma.
items: Write the complete new sentence.
Decide whether a comma is needed.
we_do.footer: Stem: In silence tells us how
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: The class listened in silence. No comma is needed.
1. SAY: "Add in silence to the sentence, then decide whether you need a comma. Write it... chin it... show me."
2. TIME: 20 seconds, then boards up together.
3. SCAN every board. 80%+ -> ask for the reason. Less -> say the sentence together, then re-collect all boards.
4. ASK: "What does in silence tell us?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: how the class listened.
TRAP: placing a comma before an end adverbial. Fix: read the sentence smoothly, remove the unnecessary comma, then show again.
---
Purpose: guided addition at the end with complete-response evidence. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar]

you_do.title: Add the given adverbial
you_do.rule: Rewrite each sentence with the given adverbial. Use a comma only when the adverbial is at the front.
you_do.example: One done for you: We waited. + after lunch -> After lunch, we waited.
items: A) The circuit worked. + during the test
B) The class listened. + in silence
you_do.footer: Front = comma. End = usually no comma.
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A - During the test, the circuit worked. B - The class listened in silence.
1. SAY: "Use the worked example. Rewrite A with the detail at the front and B with the detail at the end."
2. TIME: 90 seconds. Work independently on whiteboards.
3. CIRCULATE: if a student is stuck, SAY: "Point to where after lunch moved in the example. Now find the when detail in A." Then start A together: During the test...
4. SCAN all boards. 80%+ -> reveal. Less -> complete A together, erase it, then re-ask A.
TRAP: forgetting the comma in A or adding one in B. Fix: name the position, then repair the punctuation.
STRETCH: Move B's adverbial to the front and explain the punctuation change.
HELP: Give both sentence openings; students finish them from the printed words.
---
Purpose: fixed-answer practice adding adverbials in both positions. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar]
you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - Add the adverbial
you_do.check_rule: Tick each complete sentence. Fix the position or comma if it differs.
check_items: A) During the test, the circuit worked.
Fronted when detail: add a comma.
B) The class listened in silence.
End how detail: no comma needed.
you_do.check_footer: Name the job and position before the comma
you_do.check_notes:
ANSWER: A - During the test, the circuit worked. B - The class listened in silence.
1. REVEAL after all boards are scanned. MODEL: SAY: "During the test tells when and sits at the front, so I place a comma after it."
2. SAY: "Tick each complete sentence. Fix any position or comma that differs."
3. ASK: "Why does B have no comma?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: the adverbial is at the end.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> compare each answer with the worked example, then re-check.
TRAP: ticking correct words with incorrect punctuation. Fix: point to the adverbial's position, then repair the comma.
HELP: read the green reason line before checking the punctuation.
---
Purpose: model the position-and-comma reasoning before feedback. [You Do | Feedback | Grammar]

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
READ each word as it appears, then connect -ULE to the photographed card meaning: small.
nodule - nod means knot + -ULE means small: a small rounded knot or lump.
capsule - caps means container or cover + -ULE means small: a small case or container.
granule - gran means grain + -ULE means small: a small grain or particle.
molecule - mole names a mass unit + -ULE carries the small idea: a tiny unit of matter; do not force a false modern split.
module - mod means measure + -ULE means small: a small self-contained unit inside a larger course, machine or system.
minuscule - minus means less + -ULE means small: extremely small.
globule - glob means ball + -ULE means small: a small round ball or drop.
venule - ven means vein + -ULE means small: a small vein that joins capillaries to larger veins.
Memory hook: Hear -ULE, think LITTLE UNIT. Pinch your fingers close together and say, "Small part inside something bigger."
SOURCES:
https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/globule
https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/venule

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Add adverbials that tell how or why, building on Monday's when and where details.
PREP: Have whiteboards ready before the I do.

i_do.title: Add how or why
i_do.rule: An adverbial tells when, where, how or why. Add the detail that answers the question your reader still has.
i_do.example: The capsule opened. -> The capsule opened with a soft click.
items: With a soft click tells HOW it opened.
The detail belongs at the end, so no comma is needed.
i_do.routine: Eyes on me - ask the missing question
i_do.footer: What does your reader still need to know?
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: with a soft click - it tells how the capsule opened.
1. SAY: "An adverbial can tell how or why. I ask what detail my reader still needs."
2. MODEL: Add with a soft click. SAY: "This answers how, so the action is easier to picture."
3. ASK: "Which question does the new detail answer?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: how.
4. ASK: "Does this end adverbial need a comma?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: no.
TRAP: adding an interesting detail that does not answer how or why. Fix: ask the question first, then choose the detail.
---
Purpose: restate the rule and extend the choice of adverbial job. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar]

we_do.title: Add the reason
we_do.rule: A why adverbial explains the reason for the action.
we_do.example: Mia paused. + because the sample moved
items: Write the complete sentence with the reason at the end.
Check that the reason answers WHY.
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: Mia paused because the sample moved.
1. SAY: "Add the given reason at the end and write the complete sentence. Write it... chin it... show me."
2. TIME: 25 seconds, then boards up together.
3. SCAN every board. 80%+ -> ask for the job. Less -> ask why Mia paused, then re-collect all boards.
4. ASK: "What question does because the sample moved answer?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: why Mia paused.
TRAP: writing the reason as a sentence fragment. Fix: attach it to the main sentence, then reread the whole idea.
---
Purpose: guided addition of a reason with complete-response evidence. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar]

you_do.title: Add how and why
you_do.rule: Rewrite each sentence with the given adverbial. Keep the whole sentence complete.
you_do.example: One done for you: The door closed. + with a bang -> The door closed with a bang.
items: A) The capsule opened. + with a soft click
B) Mia paused. + because the sample moved
you_do.footer: A tells how. B tells why.
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A - The capsule opened with a soft click. B - Mia paused because the sample moved.
1. SAY: "Use the worked example. Add the how detail to A and the reason to B."
2. TIME: 90 seconds. Work independently in your OG workbook.
3. CIRCULATE: if a student is stuck, SAY: "Point to what was added in the example. Which words answer how in A?" Then attach with a soft click together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal. Less -> complete A together, cover it, then re-ask A.
TRAP: copying only the adverbial. Fix: begin with the printed main sentence, then attach the detail.
STRETCH: Move because the sample moved to the front and punctuate the new sentence.
HELP: Give each complete sentence cut into two chunks; students copy the chunks in order.
---
Purpose: fixed-answer practice adding how and why details. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar]
you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - Add how and why
you_do.check_rule: Tick each complete sentence. Fix any missing main sentence or adverbial.

B) Mia paused because the sample moved.

you_do.check_footer: Name the question each detail answers
you_do.check_notes:

extra_task.prompt: Give me one -ule word and show how it carries the meaning small.

words_to_read_review.notes:
1. READ: "Read all five rows with me. Keep the middle of long words smooth and the endings crisp."
2. READ: "Choose your stronger preference: reading or writing reads row 1; maths or science row 2; sport or outdoors row 3; art or music row 4."
3. READ: "Everyone reads row 5. Every student reads at least two rows in the group round. Finish with one steady voice."
4. ASK: "Which words end in -ite?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: appetite, exquisite, dynamite.
5. ASK: "Which words end in -ive, meaning relating to or like?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: aggressive, successive, native.
6. ASK: "Which word uses -ule, meaning small?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: capsule.
7. ASK: "Which word uses mal-, meaning ill?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: malaise.
8. ASK: "What is the opposite of seclusion?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: inclusion.
9. ASK: "Which word measures how far someone travels on foot?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: pedometer.
10. ASK: "Which word means beyond ordinary?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: extraordinary.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The graphite inside the pencil left a grey line.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The pattern seemed infinite because it never ended.

words_to_read_new.meaning: mega- means million + hertz means cycles per second: one million cycles per second
mega- means million + ton means a unit of mass: one million tons
mega- means million + unit means one amount: one million units
mega- means million + watt means a unit of power: one million watts
mega- means million + byte means a digital storage unit: one million bytes in decimal measurement
mega- means million + joule means a unit of energy: one million joules
mega- means million + pascal means a unit of pressure: one million pascals
mega- means million + volt means a unit of electric potential: one million volts

associated_word_exceptions.reason: The photographed mega- family has only four entries; megabyte is a transparent, age-relevant million-unit derivative.
The photographed mega- family has only four entries; megajoule transparently applies the SI prefix mega to joule.
The photographed mega- family has only four entries; megapascal transparently applies the SI prefix mega to pascal.
The photographed mega- family has only four entries; megavolt transparently applies the SI prefix mega to volt.

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
READ each word as it appears, then connect MEGA- to the photographed card meaning: million.
megahertz - MEGA- means million + hertz means cycles per second: one million cycles per second.
megaton - MEGA- means million + ton means a unit of mass: one million tons.
megaunit - MEGA- means million + unit means one amount: one million units.
megawatt - MEGA- means million + watt means a unit of power: one million watts.
megabyte - MEGA- means million + byte means a digital storage unit: one million bytes in decimal measurement.
megajoule - MEGA- means million + joule means a unit of energy: one million joules.
megapascal - MEGA- means million + pascal means a unit of pressure: one million pascals.
megavolt - MEGA- means million + volt means a unit of electric potential: one million volts.
Memory hook: MEGA on a measurement means ONE MILLION. Say the base unit, then add six zeros.
SOURCES:
https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/megabyte
https://www.bipm.org/en/publications/si-brochure
sessions.extension:
1. SAY: "When you finish, turn one mega- fact into a question and add a question mark."
2. CHECK: a question asks for information and ends with a question mark.
STRETCH: Write a question that compares two mega- units and answer it in a complete sentence.

new_morph_activity.title: Make mega- show one million
new_morph_activity.rule: Write one sentence for each word. Your sentence must show that mega- means exactly one million.
new_morph_activity.example: One done for you: The transmitter runs at one megahertz, or one million hertz.
items: 1. Write a sentence with megawatt that shows one million watts.
2. Write a sentence with megabyte that shows one million bytes.
new_morph_activity.footer: The number must prove the prefix meaning
new_morph_activity.notes:
1. SAY: "Write two complete sentences. Each one must use the target word and the exact words one million."
2. TIME: 4 minutes. Work independently in your OG workbook.
3. CIRCULATE: if a student is stuck, SAY: "Point to the worked example. Which two equal amounts does it name?" Then start number 1 together: One megawatt equals...
4. SCAN four books. Accurate million link -> share two. Missing link -> add the frame, then re-check a fresh sentence.
TRAP: using mega to mean only very big. Fix: replace big with one million and name the base unit.
STRETCH: Add a third sentence for megajoule and explain what a joule measures.
HELP: Give the frames "One megawatt equals one million ___." and "One megabyte equals one million ___."

review.notes:
Why learned: the opening t is usually silent in Australian English, so the word begins with /s/.
Say it: soo-NAH-mee, three beats; remember the silent t before the s.
Link: a geography word for a series of powerful sea waves caused by sudden movement under the ocean.

Why learned: the u in -cuit is silent, so the final part sounds like kit.
Say it: SUR-kit, two beats; listen for kit while remembering the silent u.
Link: a science word for a complete path through which electric current can flow.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Add two precise adverbials to one sentence without losing the main idea.
PREP: Have whiteboards ready before the I do.

i_do.title: Add two details
i_do.rule: A sentence can carry more than one adverbial. Each detail must answer when, where, how or why.
i_do.example: The team tested the circuit. -> Before sunrise, the team tested the circuit carefully.
items: Before sunrise tells WHEN; carefully tells HOW.
Only the fronted detail takes a comma.
i_do.routine: Count the two jobs with me
i_do.footer: Two details, one clear main action
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: Before sunrise tells when; carefully tells how.
1. SAY: "An adverbial tells when, where, how or why. A sentence can carry two if both add useful detail."
2. MODEL: Add before sunrise at the front and carefully at the end. Name each job aloud.
3. ASK: "Which detail takes the comma, and why?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: before sunrise because it is at the front.
4. CHECK: Ask, "What is still the main action?" EXPECT: the team tested the circuit.
TRAP: losing the main sentence while adding details. Fix: say the main action first, then attach each adverbial.
---
Purpose: restate the rule and model two controlled additions. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar]

we_do.title: Place both details
we_do.rule: Place the when or where detail first and the how detail near the action it describes.
we_do.example: The generator started. + after the repair + smoothly
items: Write one complete sentence using both details.
Add the comma required by the fronted detail.
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: After the repair, the generator started smoothly.
1. SAY: "Use both details once. Put after the repair at the front and smoothly near the action."
2. TIME: 30 seconds, then boards up together.
3. SCAN every board for both details and one comma. 80%+ -> ask for both jobs. Less -> use the footer stem, then re-collect.
4. ASK: "What does each detail tell us?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: after the repair tells when; smoothly tells how.
TRAP: adding only one detail. Fix: tick when and how separately, then add the missing one.
---
Purpose: guided construction with two required details. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar]

you_do.title: Two adverbials
you_do.rule: Rewrite each sentence with both given details. Put the first detail at the front and punctuate it.
you_do.example: One done for you: The team worked. + before lunch + quietly -> Before lunch, the team worked quietly.
items: A) The generator started. + after the repair + smoothly
B) We recorded the result. + in the science lab + with great accuracy
you_do.footer: Check both jobs before you show
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A - After the repair, the generator started smoothly. B - In the science lab, we recorded the result with great accuracy.
1. SAY: "Use the example. Add both printed details to each main sentence, with the first one at the front."
2. TIME: 2 minutes. Work independently on whiteboards.
3. CIRCULATE: if a student is stuck, SAY: "Point to the two added details in the example. Which detail starts A?" Then begin A together: After the repair,...
4. SCAN all boards for both details and the front comma. 80%+ -> reveal. Less -> rebuild A, erase it, then re-ask A.
TRAP: placing a comma before the end detail. Fix: name which detail is fronted, keep its comma, and remove the other.
STRETCH: Move B's front adverbial to the end and repunctuate the sentence.
HELP: Give the two sentence frames with the first adverbial and comma already written.
---
Purpose: fixed-answer construction with two distinct adverbial jobs. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar]

when at the front + how at the end
B) In the science lab, we recorded the result with great accuracy.

3. ASK: "Which two jobs appear in B?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: where and how.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> colour-code the two details verbally and re-check.

grammar.header_notes: Week review finisher. Add and position adverbials that tell when, where, how or why; collect exit-ticket evidence for next week.

i_do.title: Build the whole sentence
i_do.rule: Add adverbials to tell when, where, how or why. A fronted adverbial takes a comma; an end adverbial usually does not.
i_do.example: The boat moved. -> During the drill, the boat moved carefully.
items: During the drill tells WHEN; carefully tells HOW.
The main action stays clear: the boat moved.
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: during the drill tells when; carefully tells how.
1. SAY: "An adverbial tells when, where, how or why. I can add two details while keeping the main action clear."
2. MODEL: Add during the drill at the front, place the comma, then add carefully at the end.
3. ASK: "Which detail needs the comma?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: during the drill because it is at the front.
4. CHECK: Ask, "What is the main action?" EXPECT: the boat moved.
TRAP: treating the details as separate sentences. Fix: attach both to the complete main sentence.

Purpose: compressed restatement so absentees can access the exit ticket. [I Do | Review | Grammar]

we_do.title: Beat the teacher
we_do.rule: A fronted adverbial takes a comma. An adverbial at the end usually does not.
we_do.example: I wrote: During the drill the boat moved, carefully. Thumbs down - both comma decisions are wrong!
items: Fix the two comma decisions on your board.
Then name the when detail and the how detail.
we_do.footer: Stem: The first comma belongs because ...
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: During the drill, the boat moved carefully.
1. SAY: "Show thumbs down if my commas are wrong, then write the corrected sentence."
2. TIME: 25 seconds, then boards up together.
3. SCAN every board. 80%+ -> ask for both reasons. Less -> mark the front and end positions aloud, then re-collect.
4. ASK: "Why does the first comma stay and the second go?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: the when detail is fronted; the how detail is at the end.
TRAP: fixing only one comma. Fix: check the front position and end position separately, then show again.

you_do.title: Exit ticket - add the details
you_do.rule: Rewrite each sentence with both printed adverbials. Put the first at the front and the second at the end.
you_do.example: One done for you: The boat moved. + after lunch + slowly -> After lunch, the boat moved slowly.
items: A) The team checked the capsule. + during the drill + carefully
B) The circuit flashed. + after the switch closed + brightly
you_do.footer: Exit check: both details and one comma
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A - During the drill, the team checked the capsule carefully. B - After the switch closed, the circuit flashed brightly.
1. SAY: "Use the worked example. Put the first detail at the front, the second at the end, and write each complete sentence."
2. TIME: 2 minutes. Work independently on whiteboards.
3. CIRCULATE: if a student is stuck, SAY: "Point to the front detail and comma in the example. Which words must begin A?" Then start A together: During the drill,...
4. SCAN all boards and note missing details or commas for next week's warm-up group.
TRAP: adding only one adverbial. Fix: tick each printed addition separately, then add the missing detail.
STRETCH: Move the front adverbial in B to the end and repunctuate the sentence.
HELP: Provide each opening adverbial and comma; students complete the main sentence and end detail.
